nameStory: The rugosa rose gets its name from the Latin word 'rugosa,' meaning wrinkled, which perfectly describes its distinctive leaves that look like they've been crumpled up and smoothed back out. It's also called beach rose because it thrives in sandy coastal areas, and Japanese rose after its native homeland in eastern Asia.
description: Rugosa rose is a sturdy, sprawling shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall and wide, forming dense thickets along coastlines and roadsides. This non-native rose produces large, fragrant pink or white flowers throughout the summer, followed by bright red, tomato-shaped fruits called rose hips. Its most distinctive feature is its deeply wrinkled, dark green leaves that feel thick and leathery to the touch. The stems are densely covered with straight, sharp prickles of various sizes.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply wrinkled leaves that feel thick and leathery, like corrugated paper. They're compound with 5-9 leaflets, each with prominent veins that create the characteristic crumpled texture. Run your finger along the surface to feel the distinct ridges and valleys.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, showy flowers 2-4 inches across with 5 flat petals, typically bright pink or pure white. They have a sweet, classic rose fragrance that's strongest in the morning and evening. Flowers appear continuously from June through September.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright orange-red to deep red hips that are round and plump like cherry tomatoes, about 3/4 to 1 inch across. They feel firm and smooth, persisting well into winter and providing a pop of color against snow.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Densely packed with straight prickles of different sizes - some large and some tiny - creating a fearsome armor. The prickles are sharp enough to easily puncture clothing and skin, unlike the curved thorns of many other roses.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, sprawling thickets through underground runners, creating impenetrable masses especially near coastlines. Individual canes arch outward and can root where they touch the ground.

habitat: Rugosa rose thrives in sandy, salty soils along New England's coastline, from beach dunes to roadside edges near the ocean. It's extremely salt-tolerant and often forms the first line of vegetation behind beaches, but has also escaped cultivation to colonize roadsides, fields, and disturbed areas inland. Look for it anywhere the soil is sandy or where salt spray reaches.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in May, quickly developing their characteristic wrinkled texture. The thick, leathery foliage unfurls with a bronze tint before turning dark green.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with fragrant pink or white flowers appearing continuously from June through September. The first rose hips begin forming by late summer while flowers are still blooming.
seasonality.fall: Bright red-orange rose hips ripen and become prominent, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping. The large, plump hips are the most noticeable feature as flowers fade.
seasonality.winter: Persistent rose hips remain bright red against bare, extremely prickly stems. The dense network of straight prickles on gray-brown canes makes identification possible even without leaves.

funFact: Rugosa rose hips contain more vitamin C than oranges - up to 60 times more! - and were used by coastal communities during World War II as a vitamin supplement when citrus fruits were scarce.
confusionNotes: The deeply wrinkled, leathery leaves are unique among New England roses, making rugosa rose nearly impossible to confuse with other species. If the leaves look like they've been crumpled up, you've found your rugosa rose!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Japanese rose,' rugosa rose shouldn't be confused with multiflora rose, which is also sometimes called Japanese rose. Rugosa rose is considered invasive in many coastal areas of New England, where it can crowd out native beach vegetation, though it does provide valuable wildlife habitat and erosion control.
compareHints: Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture. While swamp rose and Carolina rose have similar compound leaves, theirs are smooth and thinner. Multiflora rose has much smaller flowers and tiny hips, plus smooth leaves, making the two 'Japanese roses' easy to distinguish.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
